headline: Hidden Ocean Worlds Await Discovery in the Uranus System
meta_description: Scientists find evidence that Uranus' moon Ariel once harbored a 100-mile-deep subsurface ocean, raising hopes for multiple ocean worlds in the distant system.
summary_short: Research suggests Ariel, a moon of Uranus, may have once contained a vast hidden ocean beneath its icy crust—deeper than the Pacific.
body:
Scientists examining the fractured surface of Ariel, one of Uranus' moons, have uncovered compelling evidence that this distant, relatively small world once harbored a subsurface ocean more than 100 miles deep—roughly 40 times deeper than the Pacific Ocean's average depth. New research published in the journal Icarus suggests that dramatic changes in Ariel's orbital path billions of years ago may have generated immense tidal forces, stretching and squeezing the moon's icy shell enough to create the enormous fractures and ridges visible today. The findings, led by researchers including Caleb Strom from the University of North Dakota and senior scientist Alex Patthoff of the Planetary Science Institute, point to a moon with a surprisingly violent past despite its modest size of only 720 miles across.

What makes this discovery especially significant is that Ariel is not alone. Last year, the same research team reported similar evidence for Miranda, another icy moon in the Uranus system, suggesting that multiple ocean worlds may have existed—or may still exist—orbiting the distant planet. "We are finding evidence that the Uranus system may harbor twin ocean worlds," said Tom Nordheim, principal investigator of the study. The researchers have already mapped predictions of where future spacecraft should look for confirming evidence on the unexplored northern hemispheres of these moons.

Though scientists cannot yet determine exactly when Ariel's ocean existed or how long it lasted, the research provides a foundation for understanding how subsurface oceans form and evolve on distant icy worlds. "We just need to go back to the Uranus system and see for ourselves," Nordheim said, pointing toward a future mission that could finally reveal the secrets these frozen worlds have kept hidden for billions of years.
quick_facts: Ariel's ancient ocean may have been 100+ miles deep, much deeper than Earth's Pacific
Moon is only 720 miles across—roughly Tucson to Salt Lake City distance
Researchers found Ariel's past orbit was 40 times more eccentric than today
Similar ocean evidence discovered on Miranda, another Uranus moon
Northern hemispheres of both moons remain unvisited and unexplored
